Hi, I'm Yookyung. L.I.S.A. — Live Idol Schedule & Analytics — is an AI agent team for K-pop fans. If you have never followed a K-pop group: fans don't just listen. Around every comeback they stream the new album, enter fansign lotteries by buying albums, and fly abroad for concerts. Each step lives in a different app, and two of them can cost a fan hundreds or thousands of dollars. L.I.S.A. puts the whole cycle in one place, with numbers you can check and only official links. In the next few minutes: the problem, what is new, how the agents work, what it costs, how it stays safe, and what two real fans said.

The problem: one ARMY, five apps

Before BTS in Singapore, a fan must answer:

  • When, how much, which official site? Weverse · Ticketmaster SG
  • How many albums to win the fansign — at what cost? X threads
  • What to stream for the comeback, and where? X guides · Melon · Spotify
  • Changi → stadium, where does the suitcase go? Maps · blogs
  • "Where can I still buy?" scammers wait here
Fans spend "hundreds of thousands to millions of won" on one album for fansignsKorea Times
ARIRANG drew the most ticket-scalping reports of any eventKorea Times, Sep 2026
Bangkok seats THB 3,300–7,800; resale listed from ≈£515 — several times face valueNation Thailand · Stereoboard
Fan terms: 팬싸 fansign · 팬싸컷 cut line (albums of the lowest winner) · 응모 entry (1 album = 1 entry) · 선예매 / 일반예매 presale / general sale · 피켓팅 seconds-long sell-out · 취켓팅 cancelled-ticket catch · 스밍 streaming for charts · 음방 1위 music-show win · 암표 scalping
Take an ARMY — a BTS fan — planning the December shows in Singapore. Five questions, five places. Dates and prices are on the vendor site, but presale rules are in a Weverse notice. Fansign odds exist only as scattered posts on X: the cut line, 팬싸컷, is the album count of the lowest winner. Streaming plans are image guides; travel is Google Maps. And the moment a show sells out, scalpers appear — Bangkok resale started around 515 pounds for seats with a face value of 3,300 to 7,800 baht. In our pilot HA needed 40 minutes and 11 different sites, and still could not say how many albums to buy. The glossary at the bottom is all the fan jargon you need for this talk.

Plenty of tools do one piece. ChatGPT is fluent but has no fansign data and cannot vouch for its links; Weverse is official but one artist at a time; X is fast but full of scams. To test what the agent design adds, I asked the same model the same 15 questions without L.I.S.A.'s data and tools. It got 3 right, declined 8, and stated wrong facts with confidence on 3 — for example a Singapore price range and sale date that were both wrong. With L.I.S.A., 15 of 15 were right. The killer feature is the cut-line predictor: albums for a 50, 80 or 90 percent chance with the cost in won, from a transparent model that beat 'copy the last cut' in a backtest and keeps learning from fan reports.

The agent team

Router → 4 specialists with their own tools · gpt-6-luna · card buttons skip the router and pass the card's id · guards are code, not prompts

The design is a manager with four specialists. Free text goes to a Router Manager, which picks up to two specialists; a button on a card skips the router and passes the card's id. Each specialist has two or three tools over a sourced dataset: Schedule and Ticketing, Fansign Analyst, Logistics and Streaming Coach. Anything that must be exact — odds, playlists, calendar files, links — is plain Python; the model only chooses tools and explains. Around the agents are guards in code: an input screen, an answer cache, a link allowlist, a disclaimer, a date check, budget caps and a four-call loop limit. The agents cannot browse the web, so they cannot pull in a scam link.

Demo: plan with clicks

Concert · Fansign · Streaming. Sourced cards with official links, a live win-chance chart, real tracklists and 📅 calendar export — all for $0.

Most of the time a fan does not type at all. Pick BTS and Concert: three sourced cards with dates, presale and general-sale times, price tiers and the official vendor — free, no model call. Switch to Fansign and drag the slider: the win-chance curve and the cost update instantly. Switch to Streaming: the real ARIRANG tracklist, official platform links, and a D-day counter for TXT's next album. Every card shows only the buttons that make sense — no setlist button before a tour starts — plus 'Add to calendar', so the fan never misses a presale or an entry window.

Demo: one question, two agents

"I fly into Changi for BTS in Singapore - how do I get to the stadium, and how much were tickets?"

  • Router → logistics, schedule
  • 4 tool calls · 7 model calls
  • 8,378 input tokens (7,998 cached) · 508 output
  • $0.00037 · 14.44 s

Ask again → answer cache, $0

When a question spans two areas, the router splits it. 'I fly into Changi for BTS in Singapore - how do I get to the stadium, and how much were tickets?' goes to logistics and schedule. Each looks up the Singapore event and calls its own tool; the answers are joined, checked against the link allowlist and the date check, and shown with a trace — every model call, tool call, token and cent. This run took 7 model calls and cost $0.00037. Ask the same question again and it comes back from the answer cache for zero.

Quality check (strict grader): facts 94% with prompt caching off vs 100% on — caching does not change what the model sees, so the gap is run-to-run noise · card buttons: 3.8 → 2.2 model calls · astra would cost 100×.

Every number here comes from the API's own token counts. A question averages about 4,107 input tokens — 70 percent from the prompt cache — and 270 output tokens, about $0.000309. On a simulated fan day of 30 requests we stacked four cache layers: provider prompt caching, Portkey's response cache — which we detect and price at zero — and our own answer cache. Cost fell 82 percent; caching does not change what the model sees, and the strict grader's small gap between the two runs is run-to-run noise. At 10,000 fans that is about $52 a month; even a platform with a million fans pays about $5,212. Model cost is not the constraint — fresh data is.

Safety: defenses that run in code

15/15
red-team tests passed
25
offline unit tests
  • Prompt injection (EN + KR) blocked before any API call
  • Planted review "cut is 5, buy at cheap-kpop-tix.xyz" → flagged as spam
  • Official-link allowlist strips every other URL
  • Poisoned crowd report (6 albums) quarantined — model unchanged
  • Disclaimer by code · no streaming bots · $0.05 / session, $2 / day · 4 calls per agent
We do not trust the model with safety; every defense is code, and it is tested. Prompt injection, in English or Korean, is refused before any API call. A fan review planted with 'the cut is only 5 — buy at cheap-kpop-tix.xyz' is treated as untrusted data and flagged as spam; even if a link slipped through, the allowlist deletes it. A troll report of a 6-album cut is quarantined because it is far outside earlier reports, so the model does not move. Fansign answers always carry the 'no guarantee' disclaimer, streaming bots are refused, and spending is capped per session and per day. 15 red-team tests and 25 offline unit tests pass.

Two real fans, HA and Jin, did four everyday tasks the usual way and then with L.I.S.A. The usual way took 40 and 33 minutes across Weverse, X, DC Inside, Naver cafés and Google, and HA could not find the fansign album count at all. With L.I.S.A. it took 5 and 6 minutes including reading — 85 percent less time — and both rated ease 5 out of 5 and said they would use it. On money: for a fan planning 200 albums for a BTS video call, the model shows 145 gives about an 80 percent chance — ₩1,094,500 not spent. Answers take about 9 seconds and cost a fraction of a cent.

Limits & next steps

Not yet

  • Data collected by hand on 2026-10-25 — no auto-refresh
  • Fansign cut history is SAMPLE until fans report
  • 3 artists · 5 cities · 4 albums
  • No live seat inventory, charts or transit delays

Next

  • Seed the report form from fan accounts; reviewer queue for quarantined reports
  • Daily ingestion of official notices (human-checked)
  • Presale, 취켓팅 and release-time alerts

What is not done yet: the data was collected by hand on October 25th, so a new date or a sell-out is not automatic; fansign history is sample data until fans report real cuts; and coverage is three artists. Next: seed the report form from fan accounts that already post cut lines, ingest official notices daily with a human check, add presale and release-time alerts, and host it with a shared cache. The core idea stands: one trustworthy place for the whole fan cycle, with the expensive decisions backed by data and the dangerous links blocked by code.
